---
title: "Correlations among group deviations"
execute: {warning: false, message: false}
---

The [random slope model](random-slopes.qmd) gave each MALD participant a baseline deviation and a lexical frequency slope deviation. We can now ask whether those two deviations tend to move together across participants. Recall that the [intercept](centering-predictors.qmd) depends on the predictor's zero point. The intercept slope correlation must therefore inherit that choice.

Recall that [correlation](../random-variables-and-distributions/correlation.qmd) standardizes covariance by two standard deviations; [variance, covariance, and standard deviation](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) refer here to latent deviations across participants. Conditional [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) concerns trial responses after those deviations are supplied. The resulting correlation describes how participant baseline and slope deviations vary together across repeated MALD trials.

The basic idea is to ask whether participants above the population baseline also tend to have frequency slopes above the population slope. We write the corresponding population distribution, fit it to the MALD responses, and then show why changing the intercept reference changes its correlation. The fitted participant deviations are plotted below.

## Writing one joint distribution

For participant $p$, model

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
b_{0p}\\
b_{1p}
\end{pmatrix}
\sim
\mathcal N
\left(
\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}
\tau_0^2 & \rho\tau_0\tau_1\\
\rho\tau_0\tau_1 & \tau_1^2
\end{pmatrix}
\right).
$$

The parameter $\rho$ is the correlation between participant intercept and frequency slope deviations. A positive value means that participants above the population baseline tend to have frequency slopes above the population slope. The sign of *above* depends on the response and predictor coding.

If $\rho=0$, the model treats the deviations as uncorrelated. It does not set either variance to zero; participants may still vary substantially in both dimensions.

## Fitting the covariance on centered predictors

The intercept slope covariance is one entry in the participant covariance
matrix estimated by the
[Gaussian mixed model objective](fixed-and-random-effects.qmd#gaussian-mixed-model-likelihood).
The preceding random slope fit checked the within-participant contrast and the
numerical gradient. Here we hold that model fixed and ask how its covariance
changes when the predictor zero point changes.

```{r}
#| label: mald-random-correlation
library(lme4)
library(ggplot2)

mald <- read.csv("data/mald/mald-connected-trials.csv")
mald <- subset(mald, correct == 1L)

standardize <- function(x) {
  as.numeric(scale(x))
}

mald$z_frequency <- standardize(mald$log_frequency_subtlex)
mald$z_duration <- standardize(mald$log_duration)
mald$z_trial <- standardize(mald$trial_order)

fit <- lmer(
  log_rt ~ z_frequency + z_duration + z_trial +
    (1 + z_frequency | participant_id) +
    (1 | item),
  data = mald,
  REML = TRUE,
  control = lmerControl(
    optimizer = "bobyqa",
    optCtrl = list(maxfun = 200000L)
  )
)

participant_covariance <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(fit))
participant_correlation <- participant_covariance$sdcor[
  participant_covariance$grp == "participant_id" &
    participant_covariance$var1 == "(Intercept)" &
    !is.na(participant_covariance$var2) &
    participant_covariance$var2 == "z_frequency"
]
frequency_slope_sd <- participant_covariance$sdcor[
  participant_covariance$grp == "participant_id" &
    participant_covariance$var1 == "z_frequency" &
    is.na(participant_covariance$var2)
]

c(
  intercept_frequency_correlation = participant_correlation,
  frequency_slope_sd = frequency_slope_sd
)

participant_sigma <- as.matrix(VarCorr(fit)$participant_id)
correlation_after_recentering <- function(c) {
  transformed_covariance <- participant_sigma[1L, 2L] +
    c * participant_sigma[2L, 2L]
  transformed_intercept_variance <- participant_sigma[1L, 1L] +
    2 * c * participant_sigma[1L, 2L] +
    c^2 * participant_sigma[2L, 2L]
  transformed_covariance / sqrt(
    transformed_intercept_variance * participant_sigma[2L, 2L]
  )
}
data.frame(
  centering_shift_in_standardized_frequency = c(0, 1),
  implied_intercept_slope_correlation = c(
    correlation_after_recentering(0),
    correlation_after_recentering(1)
  )
)
```

The fitted correlation is `r sprintf("%.3f", participant_correlation)`. Its meaning is tied to the intercept at mean log frequency, mean log duration, and mean trial order. The fitted slope standard deviation is only `r sprintf("%.4f", frequency_slope_sd)` log-response-time units, so a strong substantive story about the correlation would outrun the estimated slope variation.

The second table transforms the fitted MALD covariance matrix without changing any fitted response. Shifting the frequency zero by one observed scale unit changes the correlation because it changes which point on each participant line is called the intercept.

## Why centering changes the correlation

Let the centered predictor be

$$
x_i^{c}=x_i-c.
$$

Because $x_i=x_i^c+c$, the part belonging to participant $p$ becomes

$$
b_{0p}+b_{1p}x_i
=(b_{0p}+cb_{1p})+b_{1p}x_i^c.
$$

The new intercept deviation is thus

$$
b'_{0p}=b_{0p}+cb_{1p}.
$$

Its covariance with the unchanged slope is

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(b'_{0p},b_{1p})
=\operatorname{Cov}(b_{0p},b_{1p})
+c\operatorname{Var}[b_{1p}].
$$

Centering changes the point on each fitted line called the intercept. It can thus change the intercept-slope correlation without changing any fitted line or response.

For an observed participant with deviations $b_{0p}$ and $b_{1p}$, recentering by $c$ changes the intercept deviation from $b_{0p}$ to $b_{0p}+cb_{1p}$. The line has not moved. We have changed which point on it receives the name *intercept*.

For two centering constants $c_1$ and $c_2$, the same fitted group lines are represented by intercept deviations $b_{0p}+c_1b_{1p}$ and $b_{0p}+c_2b_{1p}$. Their correlations with $b_{1p}$ generally differ because the covariance changes by $c\operatorname{Var}[b_{1p}]$. Thus $\rho$ belongs to the coded covariance structure. The underlying quantities are fitted deviations rather than independently measured listener traits.

In `lmer`, `(1 + z_frequency | participant_id)` estimates the covariance between intercept and slope deviations. `(1 + z_frequency || participant_id)` sets that covariance to zero while retaining both variance components. The second form imposes an independence restriction rather than merely changing how the formula is written.

```{r}
#| label: random-correlation-plot
participant_effects <- ranef(fit)$participant_id
effect_plot <- data.frame(
  intercept_deviation = participant_effects[["(Intercept)"]],
  slope_deviation = participant_effects[["z_frequency"]]
)

ggplot(
  effect_plot,
  aes(x = intercept_deviation, y = slope_deviation)
) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey80", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey80", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(size = 1.2, color = "#1F5A85") +
  labs(
    x = "Intercept conditional mode at mean predictors",
    y = "Frequency-slope conditional mode"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

The points are conditional modes with shrinkage and unequal conditional uncertainty. Their empirical scatter helps us see the fitted group dimensions, while `VarCorr()` supplies $\widehat\rho$ from the covariance model.

A correlation near an endpoint can reflect a stable population relation or weak information in an over-rich covariance structure. It should be interpreted with the two standard deviations, the number of participant levels, and the singularity diagnostic.

## Recap and check

1. Is the empirical correlation of `ranef()` points equal to $\widehat\rho$? No. Conditional modes are shrunken and have unequal uncertainty; `VarCorr()` reports the covariance-model estimate.
2. Does `||` remove the random slope? No. It retains intercept and slope variation while constraining their covariance to zero.

We next use matrix rank to diagnose [singular fits](singular-fits.qmd).
